strings.name: Carmen Reinhart
strings.role: Harvard Kennedy School professor and former World Bank chief economist
strings.summary: Carmen Reinhart is a Cuban-born American economist studying financial crises, sovereign debt and international capital flows. She coauthored This Time Is Different with Kenneth Rogoff and served as World Bank chief economist. Calculation errors and methodological debate concerning their 2010 debt-and-growth paper also form part of her academic record.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through November 17, 2026, using an October 18 podcast listing and a 2025 Federal Reserve Bank interview for recent activity. Only the podcast description and metadata were read, not the full audio. Historical correlation is not causation, and a 90% debt ratio is not presented as a universal law.
strings.influence.rationale: Studies sovereign debt and financial crises, assembles international historical data and contributes to development-finance policy.
strings.facts.f1.label: Education
strings.facts.f1.value: BA, Florida International University, 1978; MA, Columbia University, 1980; MPhil, 1981; PhD, 1988.
strings.facts.f2.label: Scope of appointments
strings.facts.f2.value: Currently holds Harvard's endowed professorship in the international financial system; the World Bank role is former, and IMF research deputy director is not IMF chief economist.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Comparing financial history
strings.highlights.h1.text: With Rogoff, assembled historical material across countries to compare debt defaults, banking crises and currency crises; contributions of both authors must be retained.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Correction and replication
strings.highlights.h2.text: The 2013 replication identified coding, data-selection and weighting issues. The authors acknowledged a coding error but defended their central interpretation; the debate cannot be reduced to one error overturning all their research.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Debt podcast published
strings.timeline.t1.text: The episode description presents her discussing US debt, interest rates and potential risks; this is a publication date, not an established recording date or proof that a crisis occurred.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Became World Bank chief economist
strings.timeline.t2.text: The vice-president and chief-economist appointment announced May 20 took effect on this date; Gill was appointed as a subsequent permanent successor in 2022.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Responded to replication of debt research
strings.timeline.t3.text: With Rogoff, acknowledged a coding error in a figure's calculations in their 2010 paper while contesting critics' interpretations of some data handling and conclusions.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Joined Harvard Kennedy School
strings.timeline.t4.text: Became Minos A. Zombanakis Professor of the International Financial System after working at the Peterson Institute.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Published This Time Is Different
strings.timeline.t5.text: Coauthored with Kenneth Rogoff, comparing financial crises using evidence spanning centuries.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Joined the University of Maryland
strings.timeline.t6.text: Became an associate professor, later a full professor and director of the Center for International Economics.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Completed doctorate and joined the IMF
strings.timeline.t7.text: Completed her Columbia doctorate under Robert Mundell and then entered research work at the International Monetary Fund.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Joined Bear Stearns
strings.timeline.t8.text: Began work as a professional economist, becoming chief economist and vice president in 1985; these were investment-bank positions.
